newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EMU optimism gives way to worries over delay.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EMU optimism gives way to worries over delay.

text.p: European Union hopes of launching a common currency in 1999 are undergoing a serious test of political will, with tough German demands and cracks around Europe's edges raising the risk of a delay.

Following a contentious meeting of EU finance ministers on Monday which dampened hopes for a speedy accord on budgetary discipline, it emerged that Germany largest bank, Deutsche Bank had advised clients that the odds on postponing a single currency had risen.

Coming at a time when market enthusiasm over economic and monetary union (EMU) being launched on schedule was running high, the bank's investment arm, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said the odds of a delay had gone up to 45 percent from 30 percent.
Part of the reasoning behind the dour outlook is the German government's deep-seated worry over the future value of the euro, the single currency.
"While Chancellor Kohl clearly wants EMU to happen on time, he knows that to get the project up and running, euro credibility is essential," Deutsche analysts said.

But achieving credibility along German lines has become a contentious and arduous task, with the vast majority of the EU's 15 nations opposed to a too rigid application of the requirements of Maastricht treaty on monetary union.

For Italy and Spain, two countries which have come a long way from the lax budgetary and monetary policies embraced in the past, there is a strong belief that a liberal reading of Maastricht will allow them in the EMU door in 1999.
Yet despite such expectations, and with a view towards German demands, Italy has put forward tough austerity measures which have sparked a row within the governing coalition.
The Italian government urged the opposition on Tuesday to return to parliament to discuss the 1997 budget after the centre-right bloc walked out of the lower house in protest at the tough package.
Silvio Berlusconi's centre-right Freedom Alliance and the separatist Northern League announced on Monday that they would no longer attend parliamentary debate on the budget.
Their move challenges the legitimacy of any vote on a budget Prime Minister Romano Prodi says is vital to Italy's hopes of joining the single currency.
It also may reverse the recent thinking in financial markets that EMU will be launched with a majority of EU countries.
In addition to strict adherence to EMU's entry guidelines, Germany also wants to incorporate a budget stability pact that would punish states running excessive deficits after EMU.

While such an accord was expected in time for a summit of EU leaders in Dublin next month, hard negotiating tactics by German officials in Brussels on Monday have cast doubt over whether an agreement can be reached in time.
German finance state secretary Juergen Stark suggested on Monday that the credibility of such a pact was more important than timing, raising the prospect of lengthy talks into next year.
Some analysts see Germany's stubborness is more than just a negotiationg tactic to toughen up an eventual compromise -- it is a clear signal of what the German public wants.

"The position that Stark has been taking is a highly political position, designed to make sure the government will not open up an unguarged spot and allow the opposition to derail EMU," said economist Thomas Mayer at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt.
In addition to worries about political opposition in Germany, some say German Chancellor Helmut Kohl may be concerned over EMU becoming a divisive issue within his own party.
